name: evpp
baseline: libevent 2.0.21 (libevent's own sample TCP ping-pong server and client)
workload: TCP ping-pong (echo) throughput on loopback, one I/O thread per side pinned with taskset, message sizes 1024 to 16384 bytes charted, 1 to 10000 concurrent connections, evpp v0.2.4 (built on libevent 2.0.21) against libevent's server.c and client.c.
claimed_speedup: evpp throughput is about 17% higher than libevent2 when the message is smaller than 4096 bytes, and about 40%~130% higher when the message is larger than 4096 bytes. Same docs set: evpp 20%~50% faster than Boost.Asio 1.10.8 on the IO-event benchmark, about 2% slower than raw libevent there; throughput vs Asio and vs muduo described as similar.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.2 20140120 (Red Hat 4.8.2-15); tools/benchmark-build.sh uses CMake release build, which CMakeLists.txt sets to -O3 -g -ggdb -DNDEBUG; libevent 2.0.21
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2630 v2 @ 2.60GHz, Linux CentOS 6.2 (kernel 2.6.32-220.7.1.el6.x86_64)
stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; README claims production use at Qihoo 360
tradeoffs: C++11 library layered on libevent (still depends on it), own IO buffer instead of evbuffer; nonblocking multi-threaded TCP/UDP/HTTP servers and clients, async DNS, timers, thread pool; no TLS or io_uring support was looked for in this pass.
caveats: First-party benchmark (full code, compiler, flags and CPU are public, so A by the tier rules) but old: CentOS 6.2, gcc 4.8.2 and libevent 2.0.21; libevent 2.1 may behave differently. The text gives percentages only; absolute numbers are in PNG charts on a third-party image host that was not opened. The authors attribute the large-message gap to libevent's sample reading at most 4096 bytes per read, so the 40%~130% figure mostly measures read size in the baseline sample, not a faster event loop. In the same docs set raw libevent is about 2% faster than evpp on the IO-event benchmark, and Asio and muduo throughput are described as similar, so the win is specific to libevent's own sample server. Repo has had no commits since 2022-11-06. The repo's raw README.md could not be fetched; stars and licence were read from the github.com page.

name: gRPC (C++ core, grpc_bench cpp_grpc_mt)
baseline: grpc-go (go_grpc in grpc_bench); also grpc-java (java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc) and grpc-python
workload: Unary RPC with the complex_proto request scenario in the grpc_bench shootout: ghz client with 50 connections and 1000 concurrent requests (9 client CPUs), 120 s run after 30 s warmup, server in Docker limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs and 512 MB.
claimed_speedup: With a 2-CPU server: cpp_grpc_mt 69,882 req/s vs go_grpc 50,939 (about 1.37x, derived from page data), vs java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc 45,493 (about 1.54x, derived from page data), vs python_grpc 3,457. With 3 CPUs: 71,806 vs go_grpc 61,002 (about 1.18x, derived from page data) and java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc 57,418. With a 1-CPU server cpp_grpc_mt is slower than Go: 26,376 vs 34,289 req/s.
compiler_and_flags: At the benchmarked commit 14a8435: gcc:11 Docker image, g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto, jemalloc linked, Debian libgrpc++-dev (gRPC version not pinned); go_grpc built with golang:1.17
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz, 32 GB RAM, Docker containers
tradeoffs: Large dependency tree (protobuf, abseil, c-ares, BoringSSL) and long build; the C++ library also backs the Python, Ruby, PHP, C# and Objective-C gRPC packages; the fast cpp_grpc_mt variant is a hand-written multi-threaded completion-queue server, not the generic callback API.
caveats: Low confidence that gRPC C++ is faster than the baselines on current code. The record rests on an April 2022 run of the third-party grpc_bench shootout; the grpc/grpc README itself only links a performance dashboard and compares nothing. The same shootout compares gRPC implementations of one protocol, not gRPC against a different RPC system. The newest posted run (Intel Xeon Gold 6548N, benchmarked commit c4c93b3, 2026-04-22, repo discussion 559, read through a page summary and not independently verified) reverses the result: cpp_grpc_mt 74,574 req/s vs go_grpc 88,531 at 2 CPUs and 85,485 vs 117,082 at 4 CPUs, with Rust tonic, .NET and Java Vert.x also ahead. The wins that survive are against the Python gRPC server and, in 2022, against Java HotSpot at 2 to 3 CPUs. The C++ entry links jemalloc and the gRPC library version comes from the distro package. awesome-cpp tags the licence as BSD; the repo is Apache-2.0. A Python REST-vs-gRPC coursework repo (MedhaRudra/REST-vs-gRPC) was opened and not used: Python-only, no licence, its REST client opens a new TCP connection per query.

name: iceoryx (iceperf)
baseline: POSIX message queue and Unix domain socket (SOCK_DGRAM)
workload: iceperf example: leader and follower processes ping-pong 100000 round trips per payload size from 1 kB to 4096 kB; timing covers memory allocation/release and the send only, not payload construction.
claimed_speedup: Average latency in microseconds, README example output: 1 kB payload iceoryx 0.73 vs message queue 3.1 and Unix domain socket 4.3 (about 4x and 6x, derived from page data); 4096 kB payload iceoryx 0.61 vs message queue 1.2e+03 and Unix domain socket 1.7e+03 (about 2,000x and 2,800x, derived from page data). iceoryx stays at about 0.6 us for every payload size.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1505M v5 @ 2.80GHz, Ubuntu 18.04 (README example output)
stars_or_usage: 2.2k stars; README lists ROS 2 (rmw_iceoryx), Cyclone DDS and AUTOSAR Adaptive integrations
tradeoffs: Shared-memory zero-copy transport on one machine only; needs the iox-roudi daemon and loaned-sample API (publisher fills the shared buffer directly); no network transport itself (README lists a Cyclone DDS gateway for remote traffic).
caveats: First-party example output from the README, a single run on a mobile Xeon CPU; compiler and flags are not stated, so it stays C although the iceperf source is public. Latency is flat by construction: iceoryx passes a pointer into shared memory while message queue and Unix domain socket must copy the payload, and the timing excludes filling and reading the payload, so large-payload ratios of 2,000x or more are not an end-to-end application figure. Unix domain socket baseline is nonblocking SOCK_DGRAM with retry sleeps in the sender. No comparison with other shared-memory IPC (Boost.Interprocess, ZeroMQ ipc, Cyclone DDS shm). The page header says iceoryx classic is in maintenance mode, security fixes only, with iceoryx2 as the successor; last commit 2026-08-18 added SECURITY.md and a maintenance notice. The leader source file was not fetched; the measured quantities are taken from the README text.

name: KCP
baseline: ENet (libenet) reliable UDP; README also claims a gain over TCP
workload: Real-time PvP game traffic over the public internet via home WiFi: client sends a 500-byte (or 50-byte) packet every 50 ms, server echoes it; KCP (through the asio_kcp wrapper) and ENet run at the same time on the same computer and worst-case lag when the network degrades is logged.
claimed_speedup: Wiki log sample of worst-network lag: asio_kcp 291 295 269 268 231 195 249 230 225 204 versus enet 1563 1520 1470 1482 1438 1454 1412 1637 1588 1540 (mean about 246 vs about 1,510, roughly 6x lower, derived from page data; the wiki text says KCP latency is more than three times lower than libenet). README claim vs TCP: 30%-40% lower average latency and three times lower maximum latency at the cost of 10%-20% more bandwidth.
stars_or_usage: 16.9k stars; README lists use in games and Alibaba Cloud, with ports in Go, Rust, Java and C#
tradeoffs: Spends 10%-20% extra bandwidth for lower latency; pure algorithm in two files (ikcp.h, ikcp.c) with no I/O, so the caller supplies UDP send and the clock and must call update every 10-20 ms; gives up TCP fairness in fast mode; documentation mainly in Chinese.
caveats: Independent measurement (asio_kcp author, libinzhangyuan/reliable_udp_bench_mark bench_mark.md, also opened) but an informal one-off run on a real internet path (undated): no compiler, flags, CPU model or loss rate, units are not printed (milliseconds presumed), and the numbers are a pasted log excerpt from one bad-network moment. ENet's ENET_PEER_DEFAULT_ROUND_TRIP_TIME was changed from 500 to 50 for the test. The TCP claim in the README is first-party percentages with no public data in the repo. Recent commits (2026-06-20 to 2026-06-23) are README edits; the protocol code is stable. The README.en.md link in the listing points at the English README, which carries the same claim.

name: Kore
workload: Hello World text/plain response over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, measuring framework overhead only: wrk with threads equal to the core count, 100 connections, four 20 s runs per framework in the published script.
claimed_speedup: Kore 572,782 req/s (99% latency 3.99 ms) vs Nginx echo module 381,368 req/s (99% latency 24.24 ms): about 1.50x throughput (derived from page data). Same table: libmicrohttpd 533,626, Go net/http 270,253, C++ Crow 256,552, Node HTTP 112,086 req/s.
hardware: Xeon E5-1650 @ 3.50GHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04 LTS, Linux 3.16
tradeoffs: C (or Python handlers) application platform: apps are built as shared modules or one binary; per-CPU worker processes, privilege separation, seccomp and pledge sandboxing, TLS on by default, HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket only (no HTTP/2 listed in the README).
caveats: Independent third-party suite (nanoant/WebFrameworkBenchmark, MIT, public wrk script) but a single 2015 run: Kore built without TLS (make NOTLS=1) and a very early Kore version, nginx served through the third-party echo module instead of a static response, compiler and flags unstated. Later independent data is less flattering: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks (README at commit 37f10ec, updated 2020-05-06, wrk with 8 threads) lists Kore 3.3 at 85,687 req/s with 64 connections, behind Go fasthttp 159,448 and gin 95,867 at 64 connections (ahead of C agoo-c at 83,436, and Kore reaches 152,672 at 1024 connections), and has no nginx row. Kore's own README and GitHub page contain no performance numbers; the listing's claim word is only 'scalable'.
